sourceIssues.locator: Introduction, definition of λ_SSS, p.1, in arXiv 2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024, the latest arXiv version; PDF SHA-256 99b3855a…35a9); the published text, Annals of Mathematics 200 (2024), 71–122, was not collated
sourceIssues.printed: "Take λ_SSS to be the least real number such that, for any ε > 0, there are only finitely many totally positive algebraic integers α satisfying tr(α) < (λ_SSS − ε) deg(α)."
sourceIssues.correction: "Take λ_SSS to be the greatest (the supremum of the) real numbers λ such that, for any ε > 0, there are only finitely many totally positive algebraic integers α with tr(α) < (λ − ε) deg(α)."
sourceIssues.reason: If λ has the property, so does every smaller λ′, since fewer α satisfy the weaker inequality. So the set of such λ is downward closed and has no least element. The bounds that follow (Schur, Siegel, Smyth, 1.793145 ≤ λ_SSS ≤ 2) and Example 5.9 treat λ_SSS as the greatest such number. Checked on the page image. Noted by the extraction (item 117).

review.reason: Confirmed on p.1 of arXiv v2 (SHA-256 99b3855a…35a9, fetched 23 September 2026). The property "for every ε > 0 only finitely many totally positive α have tr(α) < (λ − ε) deg(α)" is inherited by every smaller λ, so the set of such λ has no least element. Its supremum has the property (given ε, pick λ in the set within ε/2 of the supremum), so "greatest" is right, as the correction says. Theorem 1.1 and Example 5.9 use this reading.

review.reason: Confirmed on pp.32–33. U^{μ∗ν_ε}(z) = ∫U^{ν_ε}(z − x)dμ(x), and Lemma 5.2(2) bounds U^{ν_ε}(w) by log((ε² + 2ε^{3/2} + ε)/(ε − ε²)) − log|w|, so integrating multiplies the constant by μ(Σ). The constant is the logarithm of (1 + 2√ε + ε)/(1 − ε) > 1, so the printed bound holds for μ(Σ) ≤ 1. The uses are μ in Proposition 5.7 and μ_± in the proof of Proposition 2.5 (p.36), all of mass at most 1, so the reach "nothing" is right.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Theorem 5.11, pp.39–40, in arXiv 2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024, the latest arXiv version; PDF SHA-256 99b3855a…35a9); the published text, Annals of Mathematics 200 (2024), 71–122, was not collated
sourceIssues.printed: The theorem defines λ_Smyth(Σ, F) using "a finite sequence a_1, …, a_N of positive numbers". The proof obtains a from the separation theorem: "we see that a_1, …, a_N must all be nonnegative", and then: "F(x) ≥ λ_N − N^{−1} + Σ_{i≤N} a_i log|Q_i(x)| for all x ∈ Σ unless x is a root of some Q_i with i ≤ N. For such an x, the inequality follows since the left hand side is finite and the right is −∞."
sourceIssues.correction: Discard the Q_i with a_i = 0, so that the remaining coefficients are positive as the definition requires. At points x ∈ Σ that are roots only of discarded Q_i, the right side is then finite, and the inequality needs an argument. If x is a limit point of Σ, use continuity. If x is an isolated point of Σ, perturb, for example by giving the relevant Q_i a small positive coefficient at a small cost in λ.
sourceIssues.reason: When a_i = 0 the term a_i log|Q_i(x)| is 0 · (−∞), not −∞. At a root x of such a Q_i that is not a root of any Q_j with a_j > 0, the right side is finite. The Dirac measure δ_x is not in M_N, since ∫ log|Q_i| dδ_x = −∞, so the separation inequality does not cover x, and the printed justification ("the right is −∞") fails. The definition of λ_Smyth also demands positive coefficients, which the separation argument does not supply. The conclusion λ(Σ, F) = λ_Smyth(Σ, F) is expected to survive the repair. Noted by the extraction (item 114), which left the perturbation as an outstanding step.

review.reason: Confirmed on pp.39–40. The separation argument gives a_i ≥ 0, not a_i > 0 as the definition of λ_Smyth requires. At a root x of Q_i with a_i = 0 the term is not −∞, and δ_x ∉ M_N, so the printed justification fails there. The repair works: discard the Q_i with a_i = 0; at a non-isolated point of Σ both sides are continuous away from the finitely many roots of the kept Q_j, so the inequality passes to the limit; at an isolated point, add η log|Q_i| for a vanishing Q_i with η > 0 small, which costs at most η·max_{Σ₀} log|Q_i| on compact parts and is absorbed by the growth (5.11) of F elsewhere. The conclusion λ(Σ, F) = λ_Smyth(Σ, F) stands; "the proof" is the right reach.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Proposition 2.5, first paragraph, p.36, in arXiv 2111.12660v2 (16 March 2024, the latest arXiv version; PDF SHA-256 99b3855a…35a9); the published text, Annals of Mathematics 200 (2024), 71–122, was not collated
sourceIssues.printed: "We may write Σ as the union of its set of isolated points with a set of the form ∪_{k≥1} Σ_k, where each Σ_k is a compact finite union of intervals and Σ_k ⊆ Σ_{k+1} for all k ≥ 1."
sourceIssues.correction: "… as the union of its set of one-point components with a set of the form ∪_{k≥1} Σ_k …". The one-point components form a countable set, which is all the next sentence uses.
sourceIssues.reason: A one-point component need not be isolated. Σ = {0} ∪ ⋃_{n≥1}[1/(2n+1), 1/(2n)] ∪ [1, 6] is compact, has countably many components and capacity greater than 1 (it contains [1, 6], of capacity 5/4). Its component {0} is not isolated, and 0 lies in no compact finite union of intervals inside Σ, because every neighbourhood of 0 meets gaps of Σ. So the printed decomposition fails. With one-point components in place of isolated points the decomposition holds (the other components are countably many closed intervals, and Σ_k is the union of the first k of them), and the argument that μ gives this countable set measure 0 is unchanged.

sourceIssues.printed: "By Proposition 5.7, we know that I(μ) is nonpositive. A countable collection of points has zero capacity; since I(μ) > −∞, we must have that μ(∪_{k≥1} Σ_k) = 1."
sourceIssues.reason: With the paper's sign convention (Definition 2.1, I(μ) = ∫∫ −log|z − w| dμ dμ), a measure of finite energy I(μ) < ∞ gives no mass to sets of capacity zero, and that is what I(μ) ≤ 0 (Proposition 5.7) supplies. The printed condition I(μ) > −∞ holds for every compactly supported probability measure, since −log|z − w| is bounded below on a compact set. It is the condition of Ransford's convention (energy ∫∫ log|z − w|), which the paper cites in Definition 2.1 but does not use.
